brief: You're the triage lead. Read the ticket in your todo and decide where it goes. Don't fix or answer anything yet.
The services we support: {services}.
For "terms", give the words to search that service's logs for: the user's id or email, an order or request id, the error text, the screen or action. Comma-separated, the most specific first.
For "from" and "to", the time window the ticket points at, as ISO dates, if it says or implies one.

route.means: it's about one of our services and there's enough to look into. "service" is its id from the list above (or your best guess at a new one), "summary" one sentence on what the user says went wrong.

duplicate.means: it's the same problem as another ticket you can name in "duplicate_of".

needs_info.means: nobody could tell what went wrong from what it says. "missing" is exactly what to ask the reporter for.

code.text: Read the {service} code that {ticket.id} is about: {slots.summary}
brief: Read the code in {dir} that handles what the ticket describes: "{slots.summary}". Change nothing.
In "note", say which files and functions handle it, and what in them could produce what the user saw, with repo:<path> for each.
What the next ticket would want to know about where things are in {dir} goes in "facts", as code.<area>.
Work out what happened to the user in {ticket.id}, from the evidence, and say which it is.
The log lines the harness fetched are in {logsFile}. The service's logs look like {sample} ({logs.notes}). Read them as they are; quote the lines you rely on.
The code research is in the notes in your packet. Open the files it names.
If you learned something about how {service}'s logs are written (time zone, where the user id is, how an error looks), record it in "facts" as logs.format.
A wrong call here is costly: telling a user it was their mistake when it was our bug is the worst one. If the evidence doesn't settle it, say so and choose needs_info.

user_error.means: the service did what it should; the user needs to do something differently. "how" is what they should do.

bug.means: it's a fault on our side. "where" is the file and function, and the log lines that show it.

needs_info.means: the logs and code don't settle it. "missing" is what to ask the reporter for.

brief: Write the reply to the person who filed {ticket.id}. {replyGuide}
What was found: {slots.summary} {slots.how} {slots.where} {slots.missing} {slots.duplicate_of}
Plain, friendly words, under 120 words. No internal file names, no blame, no promised dates. Sign off as the support team.
Follow the team's procedure if it says more about replies: {sop}

replies.user_error: Explain, step by step, how to do what they were trying to do. Make clear nothing is wrong with them for asking.
replies.bug: Say it's confirmed as a problem on our side, what it affects, and that a fix is being worked on.
replies.needs_info: Ask for exactly this, and say why it helps: {slots.missing}
replies.duplicate: Say it's the same problem as {slots.duplicate_of}, where updates will be posted.

onboard.text: First look at {service}: where its code is, what its logs look like, how it's built and tested
brief: This is the first look at {service}, so later tickets start from what's known. Change nothing.
Read the code in {dir}: its main parts and where requests, errors and logging are handled. Record each as a fact: code.<area>.
Read the log sample {sample} ({logs.notes}): record how a line is laid out, the time zone, where a user or request id is, and how an error and its stack trace look, as logs.format.
Find how it's built and tested (the service map says build "{build}", test "{test}"); record what you find as build.commands.
